title: MehZu AI
summary: Journaling, mood, habits, prayer, workouts and goals in one place, with an AI companion that reads that context before it answers, so its advice is specific to you rather than generic.

problem: Self-improvement data usually lives in separate apps: a journal in one, a habit tracker in another, prayer and workouts somewhere else. None of them share context.
So an “AI coach” built on top of any one of them sees only a small part of the person, and it falls back on generic advice.
approach: MehZu puts the main areas of daily life into one data model that the user owns, then builds the AI on top of it. Before it responds, the companion assembles a bounded, user-scoped summary of recent journal entries, moods, habits, prayers, workouts and goals, and it keeps a small memory of facts worth remembering.
The interface is deliberately calm. There are no badges or streak pressure designed to pull you back. The aim is a tool you return to because it helps.

architecture.detail: React 19 + TypeScript SPA with lazy-loaded routes, shadcn/ui on Tailwind CSS v4, Framer Motion and React Router v7.

Convex queries, mutations and actions over 13 tables: users, preferences, journal entries, habits and logs, prayer and Quran logs, workout sessions and sets, goals, conversations, messages and AI memories.
Convex Auth with email one-time passcodes and a protected-route pattern that returns users to the page they asked for.
A provider resolver picks the configured LLM (Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini or OpenAI), so chat and the daily briefing share one code path and switching models is a configuration change.
A central context builder gathers recent user data with ownership checks and bounded result sets, then hands a structured context to the prompt.

decisions.title: Provider-agnostic from day one
decisions.body: Provider selection lives in one module with no Convex imports, so every AI feature reuses it. The briefing gives reasoning models a larger token budget, because they spend hidden tokens before returning JSON.

decisions.title: Insights only from real data
decisions.body: The insights module only reports on data the user has actually logged. It doesn’t invent trends to fill an empty dashboard.

decisions.title: Memory with a threshold
decisions.body: Facts pulled from conversations carry an importance score, and only those above a minimum score are used as context. The parsing helpers are pure functions, so they can be tested without an API key.

decisions.title: Docs as part of the product
decisions.body: Product vision, requirements, UX system, database and AI architecture, decision log and launch checklist all live in the repository, alongside the code.

contribution: Design system and every screen: onboarding, dashboard, journal, habits, prayer, workouts, goals, insights, chat, profile and settings
Convex schema, queries, mutations and actions
AI layer: provider resolution, context assembly, memory extraction and daily briefing
built: Journal with history and detail views
Habits, prayer & Quran, workouts (sessions and sets) and goals
AI chat with saved conversations and a memory layer

title: MedRef
role: Final year project: backend, ML pipeline & mobile app
summary: Patients describe symptoms in text or upload a skin or chest image. NLP and CNN models analyse the input, and the app suggests which kind of specialist to see, with nearby options and a saved history.

problem: Patients often don’t know which specialist they need. They lose time going through general consultations before they reach the right doctor.
MedRef targets that first step: describe what’s wrong, or photograph it, and get a clear suggestion of which kind of specialist to see.
approach: There are two input paths. Text symptoms go through an NLP service and a trained referral classifier. Images go through a two-stage pipeline: locally trained skin and chest CNNs run first, and the Hugging Face Inference API is used as a fallback. Both paths return a structured report that names a specialist, for example a dermatologist or a pulmonologist.

A specialist service then matches by department and distance, and every analysis is saved to the user’s history. A second iteration, MedRef AI, rebuilt the client in Flutter with patient, doctor and admin roles, so doctors can review and claim high-risk cases.

architecture.detail: Flutter app for Android, web and desktop. It handles login, symptom input, image upload from camera or gallery, results and history, and detects the right API base URL for emulator, web or physical device.
FastAPI REST service: /auth (JWT), /analyze/text, /analyze/image and /history, with uploaded images served from /uploads.
Skin and chest CNNs (Keras .h5) and a scikit-learn referral classifier (.joblib), trained in a Colab notebook and loaded at startup.
SQLAlchemy models for users, referrals and feedback, on SQLite in the first version and PostgreSQL in the MedRef AI rebuild. The backend has a Dockerfile.

decisions.title: Degrade, don’t fail
decisions.body: If the trained model files are missing, the backend falls back to keyword NLP and heuristic image routing, so the app still runs end to end in development and demos.

decisions.title: Local first, cloud as backup
decisions.body: Image analysis tries the local CNNs before calling the Hugging Face Inference API. That keeps routine requests on the server, and it still returns an answer when a local model fails.

decisions.title: Every analysis is persisted
decisions.body: Analyses are saved even for users who aren’t logged in, so every response has an ID. That fixed a class of 500 errors in the results flow.

decisions.title: Roles that mirror a clinic
decisions.body: In MedRef AI, patients, doctors and admins get separate flows. High-risk cases surface to doctors, who can claim them, and admins see system analytics.

contribution: FastAPI backend: auth, analysis endpoints, history and uploads
NLP and image-analysis services, plus the specialist-matching logic
Model training notebook and model loading
Flutter client, including the role-based MedRef AI rebuild
built: Text and image analysis with structured, specialist-tagged reports
Specialist matching by department and distance
Patient, doctor and admin roles in the Flutter rebuild
next: Clinical validation. The models haven’t been evaluated in a clinical setting, so their output is guidance, not a diagnosis
caseStudy.note: MedRef is an academic project. Its suggestions are not medical advice.

title: Gohar Medical Trust HMS
kind: Hospital management for a community hospital
summary: A hospital management system for Gohar Hospital & Trust, a 24/7 community hospital in District Buner, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It replaces paper workflows with patient records, scheduling, admissions, medical records and a lab system on a real-time backend.

problem: Gohar Hospital & Trust runs much of its work on paper. Records are slow to find, handwriting is hard to read, patient history isn’t available remotely, and there’s no central view of beds or hospital-wide figures.
Each group of staff has its own pain points: reception, clinicians, nurses and administration. A system that fits only one of them wouldn’t be used.
approach: I modelled the hospital before building screens. That meant a Convex schema with indexes and validation, and a role-based permission matrix of 9 staff roles across 13 modules.

Delivery follows the clinical flow in phases: foundation, then patients, departments and rooms, appointments, admission/discharge/transfer, medical records and the lab system. Each phase is documented and finished before the next one starts.

architecture.detail: React + TypeScript on Vite, with shadcn/ui and Tailwind. A responsive app shell has a fixed desktop sidebar and a mobile drawer, plus route guards with return-to redirects.
Convex serverless functions over a 21-table schema with indexes and validation.
Convex Auth plus an RBAC permission matrix that checks every module against the user’s role.
Reusable DataTable (sortable and filterable), debounced SearchInput, StatusBadge and EmptyState components shared across modules.

decisions.title: Readable, collision-safe MRNs
decisions.body: Patient numbers follow a GMT-YYYY-XXXXX format and retry on collision, so staff can read them aloud and they stay unique.

decisions.title: Permissions as data
decisions.body: Access is defined as a roles × modules matrix rather than scattered checks, which makes it easy to audit and to extend when new staff roles appear.

decisions.title: Build in clinical order
decisions.body: Modules ship in the order a patient moves through the hospital, so each phase builds on real, working data from the one before.

decisions.title: Documented as it grows
decisions.body: ARCHITECTURE.md and a living context document record the schema, personas, UX decisions and phase status.

contribution: Convex schema, functions and RBAC system
Every module built so far, from the app shell to the lab system
